opus-5.5.text:
I think of the origins as coming from a few different threads that eventually braided together. Probably the earliest is the computer vision work, especially Chris Olah and collaborators at Google Brain and then OpenAI. Feature visualization, the Distill articles, the "Circuits" thread. The core bet there was that if you looked closely enough at the individual neurons and weights of a trained network, you'd find real, human-understandable structure: curve detectors, edge detectors, dog-head detectors, and circuits connecting them that implemented recognizable algorithms. That was a pretty radical claim at the time, because the prevailing view was that neural nets were inscrutable black boxes and the best you could do was saliency maps or probing.

The second thread is the shift to language models. Once transformers took over, people at Anthropic and elsewhere started doing the same kind of work on attention-only toy transformers. That's where you get induction heads, the mathematical framework for transformer circuits, and the realization that some of these mechanisms are surprisingly clean and universal across models.

Then the third piece, which I think is what really turned it from a niche research program into something that could scale, is the superposition story. People noticed that neurons are polysemantic: a single neuron fires for a bunch of unrelated things. The toy models of superposition work gave a theory for why: models represent more features than they have dimensions, packing them in as nearly-orthogonal directions. That reframed the problem. The neuron isn't the right unit of analysis; the feature is. And that led directly to sparse autoencoders and dictionary learning as a way to pull those features back out, which is what made it possible to start doing interpretability on frontier-scale models rather than just toys.

So I'd describe the field's origin as a scientific conviction, almost an aesthetic one, that these systems have discoverable internal structure, combined with a safety motivation: if we're going to trust these models with important decisions, we need to understand what's actually happening inside them, not just observe their outputs. That combination of "this is beautiful science" and "this really matters" is still what drives a lot of people in the field, and it's a big part of why we started Goodfire.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, mechanistic interpretability didn't really appear out of nowhere—it grew out of a frustration that a lot of people in deep learning shared around the mid-2010s. We had these models that were working astonishingly well, and the dominant attitude was almost to shrug and say, "it's a black box, the loss goes down, who cares what's inside." And a handful of people found that genuinely unsatisfying. Not just scientifically, but from a safety perspective. If you're going to deploy systems that increasingly make consequential decisions, "it works and we don't know why" is a pretty uncomfortable place to sit.

So the early roots, in my mind, come from the vision work. People started visualizing what individual neurons in convolutional networks responded to, and they found this surprisingly rich structure—curve detectors, edge detectors, things that looked like the model had rediscovered concepts from classical computer vision and neuroscience. Chris Olah and the folks around him really pushed on that, and the Distill-era work on feature visualization and then circuits in InceptionV1 was, I think, the moment the field got a name and an identity. The key move was treating a neural network less like a statistical object and more like a piece of compiled code you could reverse engineer. The weights are the program; you just don't have the source.

That reverse-engineering framing is also why it borrowed so heavily from neuroscience and from biology more broadly. Neuroscientists had spent decades poking at neurons to figure out what they encoded, and interpretability inherited both their techniques and their humility. The difference, of course, is that with an artificial network you have perfect access—you can read every weight, run any input, ablate anything you want. So in some ways it's neuroscience with the experimental constraints removed, which makes it a much more tractable science.

Then when transformers took over, the whole question shifted from vision to language, and that's when the field really matured. Work on induction heads, on superposition, on dictionary learning and sparse autoencoders—those were attempts to deal with the fact that these models don't neatly store one concept per neuron. They pack many features into fewer dimensions than you'd expect, which is exactly what makes them hard to read and also exactly what makes them interesting.

So if I had to compress it: mechanistic interpretability started as a scientific curiosity about what neural networks actually learn, got sharpened by safety concerns into something more urgent, and became a field when people committed to the idea that these systems are understandable in principle, even if that understanding is hard to earn. I find that bet pretty compelling. It's the difference between treating models as oracles and treating them as artifacts we built and are therefore obligated to understand.

astra-6.text:
I think of mechanistic interpretability as growing out of a very basic question: we train these neural networks, and they learn to do remarkable things, but what have they actually learned? Can we open them up and understand the computation, rather than just describe their behavior?

There are several intellectual roots. One is neuroscience: trying to understand a complex system by studying its parts and how they interact. Another is the broader tradition of interpreting machine learning models. Work on visualizing features in image networks helped make the idea tangible—you could look inside a network and start to see structure.

The mechanistic ambition is to go further. Rather than saying, “This neuron seems associated with this concept,” you want to explain how particular components work together to produce a behavior, and then test that explanation by intervening on them.

AI safety has also been a strong motivation. If we're going to rely on increasingly capable systems, we'd like some way to understand what they're doing internally. So I wouldn't describe it as having one clean origin. It's a convergence of scientific curiosity, techniques for studying neural networks, and the practical need to understand systems we're building.

r001.rationale: The response mentions neuroscience and feature-visualization work as intellectual roots, but does not state that internal studies of neural networks date back to their earliest development.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify Chris Olah and Nick Cammarata at OpenAI as the tentative founders.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of mechanistic interpretability as coming out of a few different traditions, rather than having one clean starting point. People have long wanted to understand what neural networks learn, and some of the early work was very visual: looking at which inputs activate a neuron, or what kinds of features emerge inside a vision model.

The shift toward mechanistic interpretability was to ask a more specific question: can we reverse-engineer the computation? Instead of saying, “This neuron seems to respond to curves,” can we explain how a collection of neurons and connections implements a particular behavior—and then test that explanation by intervening on the network?

One influential thread was the work on circuits in vision models. Another came from the AI safety community, where understanding a model’s internal reasoning seemed potentially important for figuring out whether we could trust it. Those threads converged around this idea that a neural network is a learned program, and that we might be able to understand that program by studying its parts.

So I’d distinguish the broader ambition, which is quite old, from the particular research agenda: finding internal mechanisms, making causal claims about them, and checking whether those claims actually explain what the model does.
